# Chapter 5 — The Gate at the Door

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
This is where the series stops being an argument about what *ought* to be true
and becomes a thing that accepts or refuses a change. Server-side hooks turn
every rule the earlier books argued for into code that runs at the moment of
the commit, and the teams that hold authority are not curated by hand but
computed from the organizational coordinate. Governance stops depending on
diligence and becomes a property of the substrate itself.
:::

## From Argument to Enforcement

Everything in the earlier books was, in a sense, an argument about what ought
to be true. Names ought to conform. Authority ought to follow the
organizational coordinate. Markings that do not belong in canon ought never
to land in it. Scripts that govern the estate ought to be signed. Arguments
about what *ought* to be true are the substance of governance, but they are
also its weakness, because an argument cannot stop a commit. A gate can.

> The server-side hook is where the entire series stops being a position paper
> and becomes a thing that either accepts your change or refuses it.

## What the Gate Checks

At the moment a push arrives, before a single object becomes canon, the host
runs the rules. None of this is advisory:

| Rule enforced at the commit | What it prevents |
| :--- | :--- |
| Protected-branch changes require stewardship | Unauthorized edits to binding canon |
| Frontmatter must validate against the schema | Malformed or untraceable canon documents |
| Filenames must match the convention | Corpus the substrate can no longer navigate |
| Disallowed markings are refused | Content that has no place in the governance record |
| Scripts must carry a trusted signature | Unsigned code governing the estate |

## The Inversion

This is the inversion the series has been circling from the first book. For
decades the organizational structure lived in people's heads and in the
tribal knowledge of whoever had been there longest, enforced — when it was
enforced at all — by review, by habit, by the hope that everyone remembered
the rule. Here the rule is the gate. The coordinate is not a label that a
careful operator remembers to apply; it is a condition the commit must satisfy
to become real.

> Governance stops being a practice that depends on diligence and becomes a
> property of the substrate itself.

## Authority Maintained by the Path, Not by Hand

And the authority behind the gate is not maintained by hand. The teams that
decide who may steward, who may write, and who may only read are not lists an
administrator curates and forgets to prune. They are the organizational
coordinate, arriving as it always does: a group claim from the modern tenant
becomes team membership on the host, and a mover event in the HR feed
propagates to repository permission within minutes, without anyone touching
the Git service at all. When someone changes roles, their power over canon
changes with them, automatically, because the path computes it.

The host now holds canon, faces the network through one watched door, runs
under an identity the directory issues, and enforces the governance corpus at
the instant of the commit. What remains is to say plainly that this is real —
and to point to where it is built.
